question: A 45-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with hypertension (BP 152/96 mmHg). Which set of baseline investigations is MOST appropriate as a mandatory first-line workup?

answers.text: Fasting blood glucose, serum creatinine, urine dipstick for protein, serum electrolytes, fasting lipid profile, and ECG

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These constitute the standard mandatory baseline investigations in every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient — they screen for diabetes, renal impairment, proteinuria, dyselectrolytaemia, dyslipidaemia, and hypertensive cardiac changes.

answers.text: CT angiography of the renal arteries and plasma renin/aldosterone ratio

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are second-line investigations reserved for suspected secondary hypertension (e.g., renovascular disease, primary hyperaldosteronism). They are not routine baseline tests for a newly diagnosed hypertensive patient.
ABPM is a useful adjunct when white-coat or masked hypertension is suspected, but it does not substitute for the biochemical and cardiac baseline workup required in every new hypertensive patient.
These are selected second-line investigations for specific indications (suspected LVH, renal artery stenosis). ECG — not echocardiogram — is the mandatory cardiac screening tool at baseline.

overallFeedback.feedback: The mandatory baseline workup covers metabolic risk (glucose, lipids), renal function (creatinine, urine protein), electrolytes, and cardiac assessment (ECG). Reserve imaging and hormonal tests for suspected secondary causes.

Excellent. The mandatory baseline panel (glucose, creatinine, urine protein, electrolytes, lipids, ECG) is required in every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient before adding targeted investigations.
